meta.title: LangGraph in Depth
meta.thesis: LangGraph in Depth is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: An incident triage agent needs explicit state, branching, retries, and human approval. By the end, they should be able to build or review LangGraph state machine with conditional edges and durable checkpoints, measure correct branch chosen after failed tool calls, and catch the failure where state updates are incomplete, so later nodes make decisions from stale data.

mentalMap.title: LangGraph in Depth: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Teach LangGraph as explicit state-machine control for agents: state schema, nodes, edges, checkpoints, interrupts, and tested routes.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: LangGraph is the right lesson when agent behavior must be modeled as inspectable, resumable control flow rather than an opaque loop.

modules.title: StateGraph makes control flow visible
modules.sub: Nodes and edges replace an opaque agent loop.
modules.summary: LangGraph gives agent apps named state transitions.
objectives: Define StateGraph, nodes, edges, START, and END.
Choose graph control for branchy workflows.

blocks.title: A graph is a contract for state movement

spans.text: Problem anchor: a tutor must retrieve sources, answer, run a citation check, and ask for human review when the check fails. A single loop hides those stages. A graph names them.
LangGraph nodes read and update shared state; edges decide the next node. The compiled graph runs until END, and checkpoints can persist thread state.
If every step is linear and deterministic, a simple chain may be enough.

blocks.analogy: LangGraph is a subway map for agent state.

spans.text: State fields include question, evidence, draft, review_status, and final_answer. Nodes retrieve, draft, review, and either finish or request revision.
The graph makes the failure branch visible: unsupported citations route back to retrieval or revision instead of slipping into final output.

items.text: Write one node per meaningful transformation.

blocks.title: Graph fit
blocks.prompt: What makes LangGraph a good fit?

options.text: The app only needs one text completion.
The app needs explicit state transitions, branching, checkpoints, or interrupts.
The UI needs a landing page.

modules.title: Reducers and state shape prevent junk drawers
modules.sub: Graph state needs typed ownership and merge rules.
modules.summary: State design is the heart of LangGraph.
objectives: Use reducers or merge rules for accumulated data.
Avoid storing secrets or huge prompts.

blocks.title: Graph state is product data

spans.text: It is tempting to put every message, scratch note, tool result, and prompt into state. That creates a junk drawer. Keep exact user requirements, durable decisions, needed evidence IDs, and route status; store bulky artifacts elsewhere by reference.
Reducers or merge rules matter when nodes append messages, evidence, or findings. Without them, later nodes may overwrite or duplicate data silently.
For each field, name which node writes it and which node reads it.

blocks.analogy: State is a shared workbench; label every tray.

options.name: Secrets/full prompts
options.whenToUse: Use references or secure stores instead.

blocks.title: State owner
blocks.prompt: What question should you ask for every state field?

options.text: Can it be made invisible forever?
Which node writes it, which node reads it, and how it is merged or retained.
Does it make the graph diagram colorful?

modules.title: Checkpoints and interrupts enable resume
modules.sub: Thread IDs and persisted state make human review practical.
modules.summary: LangGraph interrupts turn waiting into resumable control flow.
objectives: Avoid non-idempotent side effects before interrupt.

blocks.title: An interrupt is a pause with state

spans.text: With a checkpointer, a graph run can be associated with a `thread_id` and resumed later. Interrupts surface a JSON-serializable request to the caller and continue when the graph is invoked with a resume command.
Avoid irreversible side effects immediately before an interrupt, because resume semantics and retries can surprise you. Put side effects after approval or behind idempotent tools.
The interrupt payload should contain exactly what the human needs to decide.

blocks.analogy: A checkpoint is a save point before the boss fight.

spans.text: The graph drafts lesson content, runs a citation check, then interrupts with the draft, sources, and risk summary. The human approves or requests revision.
The resumed graph branches to publish only if approval is explicit.

blocks.title: Interrupt rule
blocks.prompt: What should happen before an irreversible publish action?

options.text: Publish first and ask later.
Interrupt for approval with persisted state, then publish only after approval.
Store approval only in hidden model text.

blocks.explanation: Interrupts protect side effects when paired with checkpoints.

modules.title: Code a tiny conditional route
modules.sub: A small graph can make routing behavior testable.
objectives: Test both pass and fail paths.

spans.text: The model may produce a draft, but route functions decide whether the graph ends, retries, or interrupts. Treat them like production code with tests.
Spaced recall: from evaluation, hard assertions should catch missing citations or invalid schema before final output. Route based on those checks, not vibes.
Every conditional edge should have at least one test case.

blocks.title: Toy LangGraph-style route function
blocks.explanation: The code isolates review and routing so both can be tested without a full framework run.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict the route.
predictThenReveal.answer: It prints `final` because every claim appears in the evidence list.

blocks.title: Route test

options.text: Routes are never application logic.
A wrong route can skip review, approval, or revision without obvious errors.
Testing routes prevents all model drift.

blocks.explanation: Routing controls safety and completion paths.

modules.title: Test graphs as workflows, not prompts
modules.sub: Production confidence comes from path coverage and traces.
objectives: Trace state updates and tool calls.

blocks.title: The graph trace is the lesson artifact

spans.text: Trace representative runs and assert that retrieval, review, approval, and final nodes appear when expected. Compare graph outcomes against a simpler baseline to justify complexity.
Failure modes include junk-drawer state, wrong conditional routes, non-idempotent side effects before interrupts, stale checkpoints, and overlong state histories.
A release run should show path, state diff, tool calls, interrupt payload, and final output.
Review the graph trace with final answer.

items.text: State schema fields have owners, readers, and retention rules.
Every conditional route has pass and fail tests.
Checkpoints and thread IDs resume the intended run.
Interrupts happen before risky side effects with reviewable payloads.
Final claims are supported by evidence carried through state.

blocks.title: Graph release
blocks.prompt: What should block release of a LangGraph agent?

options.text: A clear state schema.
A trace showing a safety or review node was skipped on a route that needed it.
A checkpointed approval path.

blocks.explanation: Topology correctness is part of answer correctness.

framework.label: Framework
framework.laymanDefinition: A library or platform that provides agent building blocks and conventions.
framework.technicalNote: Framework choice affects state handling, tools, tracing, deployment model, ecosystem fit, and how much control the application keeps.

graph.label: Graph
graph.laymanDefinition: A workflow shape where nodes and edges define how work moves between steps.
graph.technicalNote: Graph-based agents make branching, retries, checkpoints, and human review more explicit than a single loose loop.

checkpoint.label: Checkpoint
checkpoint.laymanDefinition: A saved workflow state that lets execution resume or be inspected later.
checkpoint.technicalNote: Checkpoints are essential for durable agents because retries, approvals, and debugging need the exact state at a step boundary.

handoff.label: Handoff
handoff.laymanDefinition: Passing work from one agent, tool, or human role to another.
handoff.technicalNote: Handoffs need a typed payload, ownership transfer, stop condition, and audit trail so context does not vanish between actors.

sdk.label: SDK
sdk.laymanDefinition: A software development kit with APIs and helpers for building applications.
sdk.technicalNote: Agent SDKs encode assumptions about models, tools, sessions, tracing, and deployment, so evaluate those assumptions against the product architecture.

orchestration.label: Orchestration
orchestration.laymanDefinition: Coordinating steps, agents, tools, state, and decisions in a workflow.
orchestration.technicalNote: Orchestration owns sequencing, parallelism, retries, timeouts, approvals, and failure visibility across the agent system.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: A StateGraph node receives the current state and returns `{"status": "approved"}`. The state also has a `count` field that the node never touches. What happens to `count` after this node runs?

options.text: It is deleted, because the node didn't include it in the return value.
It is preserved unchanged, because LangGraph merges partial updates into the existing state.
It is reset to its default value defined in the schema.
The graph raises an error for the missing field.

questions.explanation: LangGraph applies partial state updates — a node only needs to return the fields it changed, and all other fields carry over untouched.

questions.prompt: You want every tool call result to be appended to a `tool_outputs` list rather than overwriting it. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Store tool outputs in a separate global variable outside the graph.
Attach a reducer (e.g., `operator.add`) to the `tool_outputs` field so each update appends instead of replaces.
Return the full accumulated list from every node manually.
Use a larger context window so the prompt holds all previous outputs.

questions.explanation: Reducers tell LangGraph how to combine a new value with the existing field value — `operator.add` on a list means append, not overwrite.

questions.prompt: A human-approval step uses `interrupt()` before sending an email. The graph is replayed after approval. Why is it important that the email-sending side effect happens AFTER the interrupt, not before?

options.text: Emails sent before the interrupt will be encrypted by the checkpointer.
Side effects before an interrupt may re-execute on replay, causing duplicate emails.
The interrupt automatically rolls back any side effects that preceded it.
LangGraph blocks network calls before an interrupt is resolved.

questions.explanation: When a graph resumes from a checkpoint, nodes before the interrupt can be re-run, so non-idempotent actions like sending an email must come after the interrupt to avoid duplicates.

questions.prompt: Write the Python return value a conditional routing function should produce to direct the graph to a node called `"escalate"` instead of `"auto_approve"`.
questions.acceptableAnswer: The function should return the string "escalate" (e.g., `return "escalate"`). LangGraph uses this returned string to look up the matching edge and move execution to the `escalate` node.
questions.explanation: A conditional edge routing function returns a string that matches one of the edge targets registered with `add_conditional_edges`.

questions.prompt: When writing tests for a LangGraph workflow, which of the following best validates that a human-approval interrupt works correctly?

options.text: Mock the LLM and assert the final output string matches expected text.
Run the graph, confirm it pauses at the interrupt, supply a resume value, then assert the post-approval node executed.
Check that the graph compiles without errors using `graph.compile()`.
Verify the system prompt contains the word 'approve'.

questions.explanation: Testing interrupts requires actually running the graph to the pause point, then resuming with a value and asserting that downstream nodes ran — compile-time checks alone can't catch runtime flow errors.
